back: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length equals the radius.[fig:1.8-A01]
extra:
Why: the circumference is \(2\pi r\), so a full turn contains \(2\pi\) arcs of length \(r\), which is \(2\pi\) radians.
One radian is about \(57.3^\circ\).

Why: a full turn is \(2\pi\) radians and also \(360^\circ\).
Example: \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) radians is \(90^\circ\).

front: How do you convert an angle from degrees to radians?
extra:
Why: \(180^\circ = \pi\) radians, so \(1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180}\) radians.
Example: \(135^\circ = \dfrac{135\pi}{180} = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).

front: How do you convert an angle from radians to degrees?
extra:
Why: \(\pi\) radians \(= 180^\circ\), so 1 radian \(= \left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^\circ \approx 57.3^\circ\).
Example: \(\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \dfrac{5 \times 180^\circ}{6} = 150^\circ\).

front: How are \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) defined using the unit circle?
back:
For the point P on the unit circle where [OP] makes the angle \(\theta\) anticlockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis:
\(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of P
\(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of P
extra: Why: for an acute angle this agrees with right-angled triangle trigonometry, because the hypotenuse OP has length 1.[fig:1.8-C01]Every point on the unit circle has coordinates between \(-1\) and 1, so \(-1 \leq \cos\theta \leq 1\) and \(-1 \leq \sin\theta \leq 1\).

Why: \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of P, which is positive above the \(x\)-axis, for \(0 \lt \theta \lt \pi\).
Memory aid: ASTC (All, Sin, Tan, Cos), anticlockwise from the 1st quadrant.

Why: \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of P, which is positive to the right of the \(y\)-axis.
Memory aid: ASTC (All, Sin, Tan, Cos), anticlockwise from the 1st quadrant.

Why: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) is positive when \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\) have the same sign: both positive in the 1st quadrant, both negative in the 3rd.
Memory aid: ASTC (All, Sin, Tan, Cos), anticlockwise from the 1st quadrant.

Why: adding \(2\pi\) is one full turn, which brings P back to the same point.
So \(\sin(\theta + 2k\pi) = \sin\theta\) for \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\).
In degrees: \(360^\circ\).

Why: adding \(2\pi\) is one full turn, which brings P back to the same point.
So \(\cos(\theta + 2k\pi) = \cos\theta\) for \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\).
In degrees: \(360^\circ\).

Why: adding \(\pi\) moves P to the opposite point \((-\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)\), and \(\dfrac{-\sin\theta}{-\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\).
So \(\tan(\theta + k\pi) = \tan\theta\) for \(k \in \mathbb{Z}\).
In degrees: \(180^\circ\).
Why: the point for \(\pi - \theta\) is the reflection of P in the \(y\)-axis, so it has the same \(y\)-coordinate.[fig:1.8-C04]Example: \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \sin\frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\).

Why: the point for \(\pi - \theta\) is the reflection of P in the \(y\)-axis, so it has the opposite \(x\)-coordinate.[fig:1.8-C04]Also: \(\tan(\pi - \theta) = -\tan\theta\).
Example: \(\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}\).

Why: the point for \(-\theta\) is the reflection of P in the \(x\)-axis, so it has the opposite \(y\)-coordinate.[fig:1.8-C05]Also: \(\tan(-\theta) = -\tan\theta\).
Example: \(\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\sin\frac{\pi}{6} = -\frac{1}{2}\).

Why: the point for \(-\theta\) is the reflection of P in the \(x\)-axis, so it has the same \(x\)-coordinate.[fig:1.8-C05]Example: \(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\).

Why: it is the \(y\)-coordinate of the point \((1, 0)\) at angle \(0\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\sin 0^\circ = 0\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\sin\pi = \sin 2\pi = 0\).

Why: it is the \(y\)-coordinate of the point \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\sin\frac{5\pi}{6} = \frac{1}{2}\).

Why: it is the \(y\)-coordinate of the point \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\sin 45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\sin\frac{3\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).
This is also written as \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Why: it is the \(y\)-coordinate of the point \(\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

Why: it is the \(y\)-coordinate of the point \((0, 1)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\sin 90^\circ = 1\).
No other angle in \([0, 2\pi]\) has this value.

Why: it is the \(x\)-coordinate of the point \((1, 0)\) at angle \(0\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\cos 0^\circ = 1\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\cos 2\pi = 1\).

Why: it is the \(x\)-coordinate of the point \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\cos\frac{11\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

Why: it is the \(x\)-coordinate of the point \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\cos 45^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\cos\frac{7\pi}{4} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).
This is also written as \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\).

Why: it is the \(x\)-coordinate of the point \(\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\cos\frac{5\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\).

Why: it is the \(x\)-coordinate of the point \((0, 1)\) at angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) on the unit circle.
In degrees: \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\cos\frac{3\pi}{2} = 0\).

Why: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), and the point at \(0\) on the unit circle is \((1, 0)\).
In degrees: \(\tan 0^\circ = 0\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\tan\pi = \tan 2\pi = 0\).

Why: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), and the point at \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) on the unit circle is \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\).
In degrees: \(\tan 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\tan\frac{7\pi}{6} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\).
This is also written as \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

Why: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), and the point at \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) on the unit circle is \(\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right)\).
In degrees: \(\tan 45^\circ = 1\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\tan\frac{5\pi}{4} = 1\).

Why: \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\), and the point at \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) on the unit circle is \(\left(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\).
In degrees: \(\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}\).
The same value in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\tan\frac{4\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\).

Why: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{2} = \dfrac{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}{\cos\frac{\pi}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{0}\), and division by zero is undefined. The line OP is vertical, so it has no gradient.
In degrees: \(\tan 90^\circ\) is undefined.
The same in \([0, 2\pi]\): \(\tan\frac{3\pi}{2}\) is also undefined.

front: How can you work out the exact values for \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) if you forget them?
back:
Draw the two special right-angled triangles and read off the ratios:
sides 1, 1 and \(\sqrt{2}\), with angles \(\frac{\pi}{4}\)
sides 1, \(\sqrt{3}\) and 2, with angles \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{3}\)[fig:1.8-D16]
extra:
Why: a right-angled isosceles triangle with legs 1 has hypotenuse \(\sqrt{2}\). An equilateral triangle with sides 2, cut in half by its altitude, gives sides 1, \(\sqrt{3}\) and 2.
Example: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{1} = \sqrt{3}\).

front: How do you find the exact value of a trigonometric ratio for an angle outside the first quadrant?
back:
1. Find the reference angle: the acute angle between [OP] and the \(x\)-axis
2. Take the exact value for the reference angle
3. Apply the sign for the quadrant
extra: Why: points on the unit circle that are reflections of each other have coordinates of the same size; only the signs differ.[fig:1.8-D17]Example: \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\) is in the 3rd quadrant with reference angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\), so \(\cos\frac{4\pi}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}\).

front: The point on the unit circle at the angle \(\pi\) is {{c1::\((-1, 0)\)}}
extra:
Why: the angle \(\pi\) points along the negative \(x\)-axis, a distance 1 from the origin.[fig:1.8-D18]So \(\cos\pi = -1\), \(\sin\pi = 0\) and \(\tan\pi = 0\).
In degrees: \(180^\circ\).

front: The point on the unit circle at the angle \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) is {{c1::\((0, -1)\)}}
extra:
Why: the angle \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) points along the negative \(y\)-axis, a distance 1 from the origin.[fig:1.8-D18]So \(\cos\frac{3\pi}{2} = 0\), \(\sin\frac{3\pi}{2} = -1\), and \(\tan\frac{3\pi}{2}\) is undefined.
In degrees: \(270^\circ\).

Why: the point \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) lies on the unit circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\).
Example: if \(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}\), then \(\cos^2\theta = 1 - \frac{9}{25} = \frac{16}{25}\).
In the formula booklet, but worth knowing by heart.

front: How do you find the other trigonometric ratios when one ratio and the quadrant of \(\theta\) are known?
back:
1. Use \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\) to find the other of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\), with \(\pm\)
2. Choose the sign from the quadrant
3. Find \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\)
extra:
Why: the identity gives the size of the ratio but not its sign; the quadrant decides the sign.
If \(\tan\theta\) is given, substitute \(\sin\theta = \tan\theta\cos\theta\) into the identity.
Example: \(\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}\) in the 2nd quadrant gives \(\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\tan\theta = -\frac{3}{4}\).

front: If one solution of \(\sin\theta = k\) is \(\theta = \alpha\), what is the other solution in \([0, 2\pi]\)?
extra: Why: the line \(y = k\) meets the unit circle at two points that are reflections of each other in the \(y\)-axis.[fig:1.8-F01]Example: \(\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2}\) gives \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}\) or \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\).

front: If one solution of \(\cos\theta = k\) is \(\theta = \alpha\), what is the other solution in \([0, 2\pi]\)?
extra: Why: the line \(x = k\) meets the unit circle at two points that are reflections of each other in the \(x\)-axis.[fig:1.8-F02]Example: \(\cos\theta = \frac{1}{2}\) gives \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}\) or \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\).

front: If one solution of \(\tan\theta = k\) is \(\theta = \alpha\), what is the other solution in \([0, 2\pi]\)?
extra: Why: \(\tan\theta\) is the gradient of [OP], and the line through O with that gradient meets the unit circle at two opposite points.[fig:1.8-F03]Example: \(\tan\theta = 1\) gives \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}\) or \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\).

front: What do you do when the calculator gives a negative angle for \(\sin^{-1}\) or \(\tan^{-1}\)?
back:
1. Mark the angle on the unit circle, measured clockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis
2. Use the symmetry rule for the function to find the second solution
3. Add \(2\pi\) to any solution that lies below the required interval
extra:
Why: \(\sin^{-1}\) and \(\tan^{-1}\) give angles between \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\); \(\cos^{-1}\) gives angles between 0 and \(\pi\).
Example: \(\sin\theta = -0.4\) gives \(\sin^{-1}(-0.4) \approx -0.412\). In \([0, 2\pi]\) the solutions are \(\pi + 0.412 \approx 3.55\) and \(2\pi - 0.412 \approx 5.87\).

front: What is the gradient of a line that makes an angle \(\theta\) with the positive \(x\)-axis?
extra: Why: the gradient is \(\dfrac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}} = \dfrac{\text{OPP}}{\text{ADJ}}\). For an obtuse angle, \(\tan\theta\) is negative, matching a line that slopes down.[fig:1.8-G01]Example: a line at \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) through \((0, 1)\) has equation \(y = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}x + 1\).
